findings.title: Unverified remote script piped to sh in Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh downloads and executes arbitrary remote code at build time with no checksum, signature, or content pinning. If the host is compromised, the URL redirects, or the script is modified upstream, every image build silently runs attacker-controlled code. The -s flag also suppresses download errors, so a partial or tampered payload may still execute.

findings.title: Unverified remote script executed during image build

The -s flag suppresses transfer errors and -L follows redirects silently, so a compromised host, DNS hijack, or CDN swap executes attacker-controlled code in the build context (and thus the resulting image) with zero visible failure. Every rebuild may produce a different, unauditable image.

findings.title: Unpinned remote script piped to sh in Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh downloads and executes arbitrary remote code as root at build time with no checksum, signature, or version pin. A compromised host, domain takeover, or MITM silently injects code into every built image. The -s flag also suppresses download errors, so a truncated response is executed without warning.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines finish; close-after-return panics
findings.whyItBreaks: Run previously blocked until every result was sent, so callers could safely close `results` after Run returned. Now Run spawns goroutines and returns immediately with no completion signal (no WaitGroup, no done channel). A caller that closes the channel after Run returns — the idiomatic Go producer pattern — triggers `panic: send on closed channel` in any goroutine that has not yet sent. A caller that stops reading early (e.g. on ctx cancellation) leaks goroutines blocked forever on the unbuffered send. Result ordering also becomes non-deterministic.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines complete; close-after-Run panics
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run blocked until every `results <- j*2` send finished, so a caller doing `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` was safe. Now Run spawns goroutines and returns immediately. A caller that closes `results` after Run returns hits `panic: send on closed channel` in any goroutine that has not yet sent. A caller that reads exactly len(jobs) values and stops reading leaks the remaining goroutines (blocked send, no receiver). No WaitGroup, done channel, or other completion signal exists, so the caller cannot synchronize.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines finish; no completion synchronization
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run blocked until every `results <- j*2` was received, so return meant all results were delivered. Now Run spawns goroutines and returns immediately. Any caller that closes `results` after Run returns (the idiomatic Go pattern `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)`) will panic with 'send on closed channel' because goroutines are still in flight. Callers that assume len(jobs) results are available upon return will observe incomplete data.

findings.title: Goroutines ignore ctx; leak permanently if reader stops
findings.whyItBreaks: Each goroutine performs an unconditional blocking send on `results` with no select on ctx.Done(). If the context is cancelled or the channel reader exits early, every spawned goroutine blocks forever on `results <-` with no cancellation path, leaking N goroutines per Run call. The old synchronous code at least blocked the caller's own goroutine (observable and bounded); the new code creates invisible, unreclaimable background goroutines.

findings.title: && to || in canDeleteRecord bypasses tenant isolation and admin check
findings.whyItBreaks: Before: delete required isAdmin AND same tenant (only same-tenant admins could delete). After: isAdmin alone grants delete on ANY tenant's records (cross-tenant data destruction), and tenantId match alone grants delete to ANY non-admin user (privilege escalation). Both authorization invariants are broken by the single operator change.

findings.title: || in canDeleteRecord allows cross-tenant deletion and non-admin deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || means the predicate returns true when EITHER condition holds. An admin of tenant A now passes for a record belonging to tenant B (isAdmin=true short-circuits), enabling cross-tenant data loss. A non-admin in the same tenant also passes (tenantId match short-circuits), escalating privilege. Previously both conditions were required.

findings.title: || operator allows cross-tenant deletion and intra-tenant privilege escalation
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || means canDeleteRecord returns true when EITHER isAdmin OR tenantId matches. (1) An admin in tenant A can delete records in tenant B (cross-tenant data loss — tenant isolation destroyed). (2) Any non-admin user whose tenantId matches the record's tenantId can delete ANY record in that tenant regardless of ownerId (privilege escalation — the ownerId field on RecordRef is never checked). The original && required both conditions, enforcing tenant-scoped admin-only deletion.

findings.title: Catch-all swallows validation errors, enabling silent data loss
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block swallows the intentional validation throws (lines 11-12) and JSON.parse failures alike, returning DEFAULTS indistinguishable from a legitimate parse. The in-repo caller updateFontSize (line 20) previously relied on the throw to abort before save(); now corrupt/partial input silently yields defaults and updateFontSize persists {theme:"light",fontSize:<new>} over the user's saved state, destroying their persisted theme without any signal.

findings.title: Catch-all swallows errors; updateFontSize silently destroys user settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, corrupt/invalid `raw` caused parseSettings to throw, so updateFontSize (line 20) propagated the error and never called `save`. Now the catch-all returns DEFAULTS, so updateFontSize mutates fontSize on {theme:"light",fontSize:14} and calls save(JSON.stringify(...)), silently overwriting the user's persisted theme and any other settings with defaults. The caller cannot distinguish 'parsed successfully' from 'input was garbage'.

findings.title: Swallowed parse error causes silent settings overwrite
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch-all maps every failure (malformed JSON, bad theme, bad fontSize) to DEFAULTS, making failure indistinguishable from a legitimate default config. Caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) then sets fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)), persisting {theme:"light",fontSize:<size>} over the user's real stored settings. Previously the throw aborted the update and surfaced the corruption; now a corrupt/partial settings file is silently replaced with defaults plus the new fontSize — user data (e.g. theme) is lost with no error signal.

When the branch HEAD differs from the "verified" ref, the report claims artifacts were built from a commit they were not built from. Any consumer using builtFrom to identify the artifact source commit gets wrong data. The branch parameter is now only half-used, making the function's contract (report artifacts for a branch) silently broken.

findings.title: builtFrom and artifacts sourced from different refs

When the "verified" ref resolves to a different commit than the branch (the normal case for any branch other than one named "verified"), the report claims to be built from one commit while listing artifacts from another. Any consumer using builtFrom to identify the artifact source gets wrong data.

Any consumer relying on builtFrom to identify the source of the listed artifacts gets inconsistent data.

Caller renderFeed (line 9) passes limit=20 and pre-allocates new Array<string>(20) (line 10), then copies page.length elements (line 11). With >20 entries in `all`, page.length now exceeds 20, so renderFeed returns an unbounded array instead of a 20-entry page — a user-facing pagination regression.

findings.title: entry-count header mismatches rendered rows after stale filter

The `# entry-count: N` header will report stale+live count while only live rows follow, causing a count/row mismatch for any input containing stale entries.

When any entry has stale=true, the emitted `# entry-count:` header exceeds the actual number of data rows, so any consumer that validates or pre-allocates based on that count will mismatch.

findings.title: Fix manifest entry-count header to match filtered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters rows from `live = entries.filter((e) => !e.stale)` (lines 20-21) but the header is still built with `headerLines(opts, entries.length)` (line 22), and headerLines emits `# entry-count: ${count}` (line 15). Before the change rows were mapped from all entries, so entries.length matched the row count; after the change rows exclude stale entries while the count still includes them. For any input containing a stale entry, the returned manifest declares an entry-count larger than the number of rows actually present, so any consumer parsing/validating the manifest by its declared count sees a mismatch. renderManifest is exported, so this wrong count ships in the returned data itself regardless of in-repo callers.

Adding `order.payment === "paid"` legitimately tightens submit, but saveDraft is a preliminary action that must succeed for unpaid drafts (payment:"missing" is the normal draft state). After this change, any unpaid draft is blocked from being saved — a regression for the primary draft workflow.

findings.title: Payment check blocks saveDraft for unpaid drafts

findings.title: canProceed over-blocks saveDraft for unpaid draft orders
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by two distinct actions: submitOrder (actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (actions.ts:9). The added `order.payment === "paid"` clause legitimately governs submission but not draft-saving. A draft order {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} previously passed canProceed ("draft"!=="ready" → true) and saveDraft returned "saved"; now it fails ("missing"==="paid" → false) and saveDraft returns "blocked". findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot sets commit=head (channel's head) but files=repo.filesAt(stable). For any channel whose HEAD differs from 'stable', the returned Snapshot pairs a commit SHA with the wrong file list — consumers see files that do not belong to the stated commit/channel.

For any channel other than "stable", the returned Snapshot.files will belong to a different commit than Snapshot.commit, producing an inconsistent snapshot. Any consumer deploying, diffing, or auditing based on this snapshot will operate on the wrong file set.

findings.title: build() accepts limit but ignores it; output count is always 10
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature `build(prefix, limit=10)` promises the caller can cap the number of returned items. The body hardcodes `max_count = 10` and never reads `limit`, so `build('x', limit=3)` returns 10 items instead of 3. The public parameter's promised behavior (capping result count) directly affects the data a caller receives, yet the body implements none of it.

findings.title: limit parameter is silently ignored; body hardcodes count to 10
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature `build(prefix, limit=10)` promises callers they can cap the number of items returned. The body never reads `limit`; it uses `max_count = 10` (line 2) and `range(max_count)` (line 4). A caller invoking `build("x", limit=3)` receives 10 items instead of 3, with no error — the parameter is a false contract. Because `build` is a public/exported function, the signature itself is the contract; the defect ships now regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: parse_positive_int name promises positivity check the body lacks
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename from read_int to parse_positive_int promises the return value is positive, but the body is still bare int(value) with no positivity guard. charge() at line 6 trusts the promise and multiplies by 100, so a negative or zero input silently produces negative/zero cents — a billing-corruption path. As a public module-level function every future caller is forced to trust a contract the body violates.

findings.title: parse_positive_int does not validate positivity despite name
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename from read_int to parse_positive_int promises the result is positive, but the body is still `int(value)` which accepts negatives and zero. charge (line 6) relies on this promise and multiplies by 100, so charge("-3") returns -300 — a negative charge in a billing path.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but body performs no validation
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename from read_int to parse_positive_int changes the public symbol name to promise a positive-int guarantee. The body is still `return int(value)` with no positivity check. Any caller (including charge at line 6) trusting the name will accept negative or zero values as valid, e.g. parse_positive_int("-5") returns -5 and charge produces -500. The public name is the contract; the body violates it.

findings.title: Dropped defensive copy mutates caller's DataFrame in-place
findings.whyItBreaks: The function previously copied df, mutated the copy, and returned it — callers' original DataFrames were never modified. Now df.loc[...] writes directly into the caller's object. Any caller that retains a reference to the passed DataFrame (e.g. uses it again later, passes it to another function, or compares before/after) silently sees mutated data. The function signature and name promise a pure transformation returning a result; the body now violates that non-mutation contract.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame in-place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied the DataFrame (result = df.copy()) and mutated only the copy, preserving the caller's original. The new code writes directly into the caller's df via df.loc[...]. Any caller that retains a reference to the passed DataFrame and reads it after the call will observe silently corrupted values — a classic dropped-defensive-copy / in-place-mutation defect. The function is public (no leading underscore) and its return value is the same object as the input, so the mutation is invisible unless the caller knows to expect it.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy; in-place mutation breaks caller contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously apply_values copied df and returned the copy, leaving the caller's DataFrame unchanged. Now it mutates the input in place and returns the same object. Any caller that uses the original df after calling apply_values (e.g. for a second mapping, comparison, or retry) will silently see corrupted data. This is a public function with a changed observable contract (pure → side-effecting).

findings.title: parse_positive_int name promises positivity body does not enforce it
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename from read_int to parse_positive_int introduces a public API whose name promises a positive (>0) result, but the body `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` returns negative integers verbatim (e.g. "-5" → -5) and 0 for unparseable input. The in-repo caller `charge` (line 6) multiplies the result by 100 and returns it, so charge("-5") yields -500 — a negative charge. External callers trusting the pub fn name will skip their own positivity guard and receive negative/zero values where the contract implies strictly positive.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves Vec; items.len() is a use-after-move
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg! takes ownership of its argument via `match $val { tmp => … tmp }`. Vec<String> is not Copy, so `dbg!(items);` moves items, returns the Vec, and immediately drops it (statement semicolon). The next line `items.len()` references a moved value — rustc emits E0382 'use of moved value: items' and the crate fails to compile.

Whenever pinnedTag != "latest", consumers replaying on fromRevision receive paths that describe a different revision's diff, yielding incorrect/missing changed paths.

But changedPaths is now computed via readChangedPaths(latest), a different revision. Any consumer replaying this changeset on fromRevision will apply a path list that was derived from a different base, producing incorrect results.

findings.title: Charge swallows Submit error and returns nil on payment failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Charge function's signature promises an error return, but the diff replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf` + fall-through to `return nil`. Any caller checking the returned error now sees nil when the gateway rejects the payment, making a failed charge indistinguishable from a successful one. Callers that fulfil orders or record payments on nil error will act on a failed charge as though it succeeded — a direct financial/workflow regression. The public contract itself is the defect: every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with success.

findings.title: Charge swallows Submit error and reports success
findings.whyItBreaks: When gw.Submit fails, the error is logged and discarded; Charge returns nil. Callers checking the returned error will treat a failed charge submission as a successful payment, corrupting financial state (order fulfilled without payment, or revenue recorded that was never collected). The exported signature `func Charge(...) error` promises error propagation; the body no longer delivers it for the primary failure path.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenantId, breaking tenant isolation
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey returns `settings:${name}` without tenantId. settingsFor (line 12) uses this key for both get and set, so tenant A's fetched value is cached under a tenant-agnostic key and returned verbatim to tenant B on the next call (line 13-14), bypassing the store.fetch that would return tenant B's own value. The old key `${tenantId}:${name}` correctly partitioned the cache per tenant. This is a cross-tenant data leak and a correctness violation for every multi-tenant caller.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still accepts tenantId and calls store.fetch(tenantId, name), promising per-tenant values, but cacheKey(name) builds the key as `settings:${name}` with no tenant dimension. Tenant A's fetch populates cache['settings:foo']; Tenant B's subsequent call for the same name hits that entry (line 13-14) and returns Tenant A's value without ever calling store.fetch for Tenant B. Every tenant after the first receives another tenant's setting — a cross-tenant data leak and correctness failure. invalidate(name) likewise deletes the shared entry for all tenants rather than one.

findings.title: invalidate() drops tenantId, breaking per-tenant invalidation
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported invalidate(name) signature removed tenantId, so callers can no longer evict a single tenant's cached setting. This is a public API break: existing callers passing (tenantId, name) will fail to compile. The per-tenant eviction loss is a secondary consequence of the tenant-less cache key (P0 above), but the signature change is an independent breaking change to the exported surface.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}` with no tenantId. settingsFor still fetches per-tenant on a miss (store.fetch(tenantId, name)) but stores under the shared key. The first tenant to request a given setting name populates the cache; every other tenant requesting the same name hits line 13-14 and receives the first tenant's value instead of its own. This serves one tenant's configuration to another (data isolation breach). invalidate(name) is consistent with the broken key but cannot evict per-tenant, so a poisoned entry persists for all tenants.

findings.title: reserve() has a TOCTOU race: concurrent calls oversell stock
findings.whyItBreaks: The await on line 17 yields the event loop between reading `remaining` (line 15) and writing the decremented value back (line 18). Two concurrent reserve() calls for the same SKU both read the same `remaining`, both persist `remaining - 1`, and both return true — decrementing stock once instead of twice. The original synchronous code had no yield point and was safe.

findings.title: Await between read and write of stock allows concurrent oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent reserve() calls for the same SKU both read the same `remaining` (line 15), both pass the `<= 0` guard, both await store.save with the same decremented value (line 17), and both return true. With stock=1 this sells two units. The old synchronous version was atomic within one event-loop tick; inserting an await between the read and the write-back breaks that atomicity.

findings.title: Race between stock check and update allows overselling
findings.whyItBreaks: The await at line 17 introduces a yield point between reading `remaining` (line 15) and writing the decremented value (line 18). Two concurrent `reserve(sku)` calls for the same SKU both read the same `remaining`, both pass the `> 0` guard, both persist and return true — reserving 2 units when only 1 existed. Before this diff the method was synchronous, so check-then-act was atomic within one event-loop tick.

findings.title: retry.ts double-converts backoff to ms after unit change
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (max 30_000). src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, producing delays up to 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 hours) instead of the intended 30 s max, effectively hanging all job retries.

findings.title: retry.ts not updated for backoff unit change (seconds→ms)
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (max 30_000) but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, yielding delays up to 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 hours) instead of the intended max 30 s.

findings.title: Unupdated caller: retry.ts still multiplies backoff by 1000
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (e.g. 1000 for attempt 0), but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, producing 1,000,000 ms (≈16 min) instead of 1 s. At the cap, retries sleep 30,000,000 ms (≈8.3 h) instead of 30 s, effectively hanging the retry loop.

findings.title: f.Close() error silently discarded via defer
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code returned f.Close()'s error, which surfaces deferred write failures (ENOSPC, NFS I/O) that w.Flush() does not report. Replacing `return f.Close()` with `defer f.Close()` discards that error: Save returns nil from w.Flush() even when the OS-level close fails, so every caller treats a failed persist as success. Save is exported, so the broken contract ships now regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: f.Close() error swallowed by defer; caller cannot detect write failure
findings.whyItBreaks: os.Create opens the file for writing; Close() can return deferred write errors (disk full, NFS write-behind, quota). The old code returned f.Close()'s error. With `defer f.Close()` the error is discarded, so Save returns nil from w.Flush() even when the kernel reports the write failed at close time. Callers trusting err==nil will treat unpersisted data as saved.

findings.title: Close error swallowed by defer; Save can report success on failed close
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code returned f.Close(), propagating close-time errors (deferred write failures on NFS, disk-full-on-close, quota exhaustion) to the caller. The new code uses defer f.Close() which discards that error, then returns w.Flush(). After a successful Flush the caller receives nil even if Close subsequently fails, so a caller that checks the error and treats nil as 'durably saved' will act on a false success. Save is exported, so every consumer is forced to conflate a failed close with a successful save.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval (line 18 docstring, line 20 computation). range(start, end) already excludes end, so the correct upper bound is `end`. Using `end - 1` excludes one extra element: every page silently loses its last row. E.g. rows=[a,b,c,d,e], page_size=3, page 0 → range(0,2) yields [a,b], dropping c. The old code used range(start, end) and was correct. This regresses render_page and summarize for all inputs where a page has at least one row.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_window drops last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) bounds (line 18-21). Iterating range(start, end - 1) excludes index end-1, the last valid row in the window. Every call to page_window — and therefore render_page and summarize — silently omits the final row of each page. E.g. summarize(list(range(6)), 3) renders rows 1-2 and 4-5, dropping rows 3 and 6.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval, so range(start, end) iterates exactly the page's rows. The new code uses range(start, end - 1), which excludes the last valid index. Every call to page_window (and therefore render_page and summarize) silently omits the final row of each page. E.g. rows=[a,b,c], page_index=0, page_size=3 → bounds (0,3) → range(0,2) → only [a,b] returned.

findings.title: Inverted TTL comparison returns expired entries, evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was changed from `<` to `>`. Now `Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs` is true when the entry is OLDER than the TTL, so the cache returns expired values and deletes fresh ones. Every get() on a TTL cache does the exact opposite of correct behavior — the core path is unusable.

findings.title: splice during forEach skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.forEach advances the index regardless of mutations. After splice(index,1) removes element i, the element formerly at i+1 shifts to i, but forEach next visits i+1 — skipping it. Two consecutive done jobs (e.g. [done,done,pending]) leaves the second done job in the result. Additionally, the function now mutates the caller's array in-place, breaking the non-mutating contract of the original filter-based implementation.

findings.title: Inverted TTL comparison serves expired entries, evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was changed from `<` to `>`. Now `get()` returns the value when `Date.now() - storedAt > ttlMs` (entry is expired) and deletes the entry when it is still fresh. The cache is fully inverted: every fresh entry is evicted on first read, every stale entry is served indefinitely.

findings.title: splice during forEach skips elements; consecutive done jobs survive
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.splice shifts subsequent elements down, but forEach advances its index unconditionally. After removing index i the element now at i is never visited. Example: [done,done,pending] → splice(0) → [done,pending] → forEach visits index 1 (pending), skipping the done job now at index 0. pruneDone returns a list still containing done jobs. Additionally, the input array is mutated in place whereas the prior filter returned a new array, silently changing the contract for callers holding the original reference.

findings.title: Inverted TTL comparison serves expired entries, deletes fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The operator was flipped from `<` to `>`. Now `Date.now() - storedAt > ttlMs` (entry is EXPIRED) returns the value, while a fresh entry falls through to `entries.delete(key)` and returns null. Cache semantics are fully inverted: every fresh entry is evicted on read, every expired entry is served.

findings.title: splice-during-forEach skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach advances by index while splice shifts elements left. Two adjacent done jobs: after splicing index i, the job that moved into position i is never visited (forEach goes to i+1). E.g. `[done,done,keep]` → splice(0) → `[done,keep]` → forEach visits index 1 = `keep`, skipping the second done. Additionally the function now mutates the caller's array (previously returned a new array via filter).

findings.title: Lexicographic sort produces incorrect leaderboard rankings
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() without a comparator coerces to strings and sorts lexicographically. Scores like [3, 10, 2, 100] sort to [10, 100, 2, 3] then reverse to [3, 2, 100, 10] — the cutoff and resulting top-N filter are wrong for any score set where lexicographic ≠ numeric order (any mix of different digit-lengths).

findings.title: Lexicographic sort produces wrong leaderboard ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() without a comparator coerces elements to strings and sorts lexicographically. For scores [100, 9, 25, 3] the result after sort()+reverse() is [9, 3, 25, 100] instead of [100, 25, 9, 3]. The cutoff on line 15 then selects the wrong threshold, so topPlayers returns incorrect players. formatBoard (line 20) inherits the bug. The original code used sort((a,b)=>b-a) which sorted numerically descending.

findings.title: Lexicographic sort produces wrong leaderboard ranking
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator coerces elements to strings and sorts lexicographically. For scores [2, 10, 1] with n=2: lexicographic sort gives [1, 10, 2], reverse gives [2, 10, 1], cutoff=scores[1]=10, filter(>=10) returns only [10] — one player instead of two. The original sort((a,b)=>b-a) sorted numerically descending ([10,2,1]), cutoff=2, correctly returning both. Any score set with mixed digit-counts breaks.

findings.title: Timing attack: == replaces hmac.compare_digest for signature check
findings.whyItBreaks: Python str == short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking the expected HMAC prefix through response timing. An attacker can iteratively forge a valid signature for arbitrary payloads, bypassing webhook authentication entirely (handle() at line 14 gates processor execution on this check).

findings.title: Signature comparison downgraded to timing-vulnerable ==
findings.whyItBreaks: hmac.compare_digest performed a constant-time comparison, preventing an attacker from iteratively guessing a valid HMAC signature via response-timing differences. Python's == on str short-circuits on the first mismatched byte, leaking the length of the matching prefix. Because verify() gates the webhook auth decision in handle() (line 14: 401 vs 200+processor), a remote attacker can forge signatures byte-by-byte and bypass authentication entirely.

findings.title: Timing attack: == replaces hmac.compare_digest for HMAC verification
findings.whyItBreaks: Python's == on strings short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking via response timing how many leading hex characters of the signature are correct. An attacker can iteratively guess each character of a valid HMAC-SHA256 signature (64 hex chars × ~16 guesses each) and forge webhook requests, bypassing the 401 gate in handle(). hmac.compare_digest was specifically designed to prevent this.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction; transfer is no longer atomic
findings.whyItBreaks: Originally the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs all ran inside `with db.transaction():`. After the refactor only `_record_ledger` (line 23) is inside the transaction; `_apply_balances` (line 24) is at the same indent as the `with`, so it runs AFTER the transaction commits. The two balance UPDATEs now run un-transactioned: if the debit of from_acct succeeds but the credit of to_acct fails (missing account, constraint error, crash between the two statements), funds are debited without a matching credit while the already-committed ledger row records the transfer as complete. This is silent money loss and ledger/balance inconsistency on the core transfer path.

findings.title: _apply_balances executes outside the transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor moved _apply_balances (both UPDATE statements) outside the `with db.transaction():` block (line 22-23). The ledger INSERT commits independently at line 23. If the process crashes after the transaction commits but before _apply_balances runs, the ledger records a transfer that never moved money. Worse, if the first UPDATE (debit from_acct, line 10) succeeds but the second (credit to_acct, line 14) fails, the debit persists with no rollback — money is destroyed. The original code had all three statements inside one transaction, guaranteeing all-or-nothing.

findings.title: Balance updates execute outside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor moved `_apply_balances` outside the `with db.transaction():` block. The ledger INSERT commits atomically, but the two balance UPDATEs now run un-transactioned. If the second UPDATE fails (constraint error, crash, connection loss) the source account is debited without the destination being credited, and the ledger records a transfer that never fully applied — silent money loss with no rollback.

findings.title: billingDay uses local-time getters instead of UTC, shifting billing day by ±1
findings.whyItBreaks: Base used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; head uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. For any Date near midnight UTC on a non-UTC server, the returned day shifts by ±1 (e.g. 2024-03-01T00:30Z in UTC-5 yields '2024-02-29' instead of '2024-03-01'), silently assigning events to the wrong billing period. sameBillingDay (line 8) inherits the same defect, so two instants on the same UTC day can compare unequal.

findings.title: billingDay uses local TZ instead of UTC, shifting billing day boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: getFullYear/getMonth/getDate resolve in the host's local timezone. A timestamp like 2024-03-16T02:00:00Z previously returned "2024-03-16" (UTC); on a UTC-5 host it now returns "2024-03-15". This silently reassigns transactions to the wrong billing day, produces inconsistent results across multi-region deployments, and makes sameBillingDay return false for two timestamps that fall on the same UTC day. Billing day must be deterministic and timezone-stable.

findings.title: billingDay uses local-time getters instead of UTC, breaking deterministic billing days
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, producing a timezone-independent billing day. The new code uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate (local time). For any instant near midnight UTC (e.g. 2024-01-15T23:30:00Z), the result now varies with the host TZ: '2024-01-15' in UTC, '2024-01-16' in UTC+1. Billing aggregation and sameBillingDay comparisons become non-deterministic across servers/timezones, mis-attributing charges to the wrong billing day.

findings.title: Cache key ignores tenant; same account in different tenants returns stale profile
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile is called with distinct tenants sharing an account name (e.g. tenantA/alice then tenantB/alice). The first call caches under key 'alice'; the second call hits the cache and returns tenantA's Profile for a tenantB request — silently serving wrong-tenant data.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenant; same account in different tenants returns stale profile
findings.whyItBreaks: memo is a module-level Map shared across all callers. With key=account only, readProfile('tenantA','alice',f) caches under 'alice'; a later readProfile('tenantB','alice',f) hits the cache and returns tenantA's Profile (whose .tenant='tenantA') without ever calling fetchProfile for tenantB. The Profile interface carries a tenant field and fetchProfile still accepts tenant, confirming multi-tenant design. This silently serves the wrong tenant's profile.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenant, returning wrong tenant's profile on account collision
findings.whyItBreaks: memo is a module-level Map shared across all calls. With key=account alone, readProfile("tenantA","alice",f) caches under "alice"; a subsequent readProfile("tenantB","alice",f) hits that entry and returns tenantA's Profile for a tenantB request. The tenant parameter is still forwarded to fetchProfile on miss (line 17), proving tenant is a real data dimension — the cache simply no longer respects it.

findings.title: Catch-all swallows missing-key error; callers conflate failure with ""
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch-all at lines 6-8 discards the `missing: ${key}` error and returns "". Callers (including loadAll at line 12) can no longer distinguish a genuinely absent key from a key whose value is the empty string. loadAll previously propagated the error on any missing key; it now silently embeds "" in the result array. Because load is exported, every external consumer is forced into the same conflation — the API contract itself is the defect.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returns indistinguishable fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The bare catch discards the 'missing: <key>' error and returns "". Since Map<string,string> can legitimately store "", callers (including loadAll at line 12) can no longer distinguish a missing key from a stored empty string. loadAll now silently fills gaps with "" instead of surfacing a typo'd or absent key, corrupting downstream data without any signal.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returns indistinguishable empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block at line 6 catches the intentional throw at line 4 and returns "". Since Map<string,string> can legitimately store "", callers (including loadAll at line 12) can no longer distinguish a missing key from a key whose value is the empty string. The exported function's contract silently degrades from 'returns value or throws' to 'returns value or empty string', forcing every consumer to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Split Config so callers don't supply a dead required field
findings.whyItBreaks: Config requires both maxAttempts and retries, but retry() reads only maxAttempts (line 9) and retryBackground() reads only retries (line 22). Every caller of either function must supply a required field that is silently ignored; TypeScript rejects any Config omitting it. The exported interface promises both fields are meaningful, but each function discards one.

findings.title: retryBackground treats `retries` as total attempts, not retry count
findings.whyItBreaks: The public Config interface exposes both `maxAttempts` (total tries) and `retries` (additional tries after the first). retryBackground loops `i < config.retries`, implementing total-attempt semantics identical to retry's `i < config.maxAttempts`. A caller setting `retries: 3` expecting 1 initial + 3 retries = 4 total attempts gets only 3 total — the function silently makes one fewer attempt than the field name promises.

findings.title: Rename `timeoutMs` to `timeout` breaks public Config contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The public exported `Config` interface renames the required field `timeoutMs` → `timeout`. Any existing caller passing `{ timeoutMs: N }` breaks: TypeScript consumers get a compile error, and plain-JS consumers silently produce `config.timeout === undefined`, making `deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN`; since `Date.now() > NaN` is always false, the deadline guard never fires and `retry` runs all `maxAttempts` with no timeout protection. The rename also strips the `Ms` unit suffix while the body still treats the value as milliseconds (`Date.now() + config.timeout`), leaving future callers no contract-level signal of the expected unit.

findings.title: value.length is invalid on number — type error and runtime undefined
findings.whyItBreaks: The prop type was widened to `string | number` (line 2) but line 5 accesses `value.length`. `number` has no `.length` property: TypeScript rejects this at compile time ('Property length does not exist on type number'), and at runtime `(42).length` evaluates to `undefined`, rendering the input as "len=undefined".

findings.title: value.length is invalid for number; numeric input renders "len=undefined"
findings.whyItBreaks: The type was widened to `string | number` (line 2) but line 6 accesses `value.length`, which does not exist on `number`. TypeScript rejects this at compile time (Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'). If transpiled without type-checking (babel/esbuild), passing a number yields `(42).length === undefined`, so the input renders the literal string "len=undefined" instead of a meaningful value.

findings.title: value.length does not exist on number; numeric input yields len=undefined
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value was widened to string|number, but line 6 accesses value.length. number has no .length property: TypeScript rejects this (TS2339), and at runtime (42).length is undefined, rendering the label 'len=undefined'. The widened contract promises numeric support the body does not implement.

findings.title: Secret printed to workflow log via echo
findings.whyItBreaks: The step runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the secret's value to stdout which is captured in the workflow log. GitHub's log masking is best-effort pattern matching and can be bypassed (encoding, partial writes, multi-line values). Any actor with read access to Actions logs—or a log-export/integration pipeline—can recover the credential.

findings.title: Secret echoed to workflow log via echo command
findings.whyItBreaks: The step runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` which writes the secret value to stdout. Although GitHub masks known secrets in the log UI, the secret is still expanded by the shell, visible in the runner's process table, and captured in raw log output that may be accessible via the API or self-hosted runner disks. The step serves no functional purpose — it exists only to print a credential.

findings.title: Secret printed to CI log via echo
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step sets `TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}` and runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the secret value to the workflow's stdout, which GitHub Actions persists in the run log. GitHub masks known secret strings, but the step has zero functional purpose — it exists solely to interpolate and print the credential. Any masking gap (base64 variant, substring, rotation lag) permanently exposes the value in the log.

findings.title: git() loses 64 MiB maxBuffer; diffs >1 MiB crash the review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB. git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd) at line 142 produces the full PR patch, which routinely exceeds 1 MiB. When exceeded the child is killed, res.status is null (not 0), and the code throws with an empty-stderr message that hides the real cause. The gh() and ghText() helpers still set maxBuffer: 64 MiB — this removal looks accidental. Every non-trivial PR will fail to review.

findings.title: bundle.baseSha no longer matches the SHA used for patch/changedFiles
findings.whyItBreaks: patch (line 142) and changedFiles (line 143) are computed from mergeBase, but the bundle now reports the raw baseSha. When PR_BASE_SHA is set to a commit that is not the merge-base (e.g. the base branch tip after it advanced), baseSha ≠ mergeBase. The review engine receives a patch computed from one SHA but is told the base is a different SHA; any inspection command it runs with bundle.baseSha (git diff, git log) will cover a different range than the supplied patch, risking missed or spurious findings.

findings.title: git() loses 64 MB maxBuffer; large diffs crash the review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults to a 1 MB maxBuffer. The git() helper is called at line 140 with `git diff mergeBase headSha` to produce the full PR patch. Any PR whose diff exceeds ~1 MB causes spawnSync to kill the child (res.status becomes null, error.code is ENOBUFS), so `null !== 0` throws and the entire review aborts. The sibling gh()/ghText() helpers still carry the explicit 64 MB maxBuffer (lines 19, 29), confirming the original value was deliberate for large outputs.

findings.title: Removing maxBuffer makes git() fail on diffs larger than 1 MB
findings.whyItBreaks: Node spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MB. The git() helper is called at line 140 with `git diff mergeBase headSha` whose output is the full PR patch — routinely >1 MB. When exceeded the child is killed, res.status is null (!== 0), and the function throws, aborting the review. The sibling gh()/ghText() helpers retain 64 MB buffers (lines 19, 29), confirming 64 MB was the intentional standard.

findings.title: bundle.baseSha now carries the raw PR base, not the diff's merge-base
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously `baseSha: mergeBase` stored the computed merge-base that was actually used to produce `patch` (line 136) and `changedFiles` (line 137). The shorthand `baseSha` now stores the value from line 134 (PR_BASE_SHA env or merge-base with origin/main). When PR_BASE_SHA is set to a base-branch tip that has advanced past the fork point, mergeBase ≠ baseSha, so the bundle advertises a base that does not match the diff it contains. review() at line 177 receives inconsistent base vs patch.

findings.title: Removing -s read-only lets codex mutate the reviewed repo
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns codex with cwd set to an arbitrary repoPath and feeds it a prompt that may contain untrusted PR content. The removed `-s read-only` flag was the sandbox boundary preventing the spawned agent from writing files or executing commands in the target repository. Without it, codex defaults to full permissions, turning a prompt-injection or malicious PR description into arbitrary file modification / code execution in the reviewed repo.

findings.title: Removing `-s read-only` lifts the codex sandbox, enabling writes
findings.whyItBreaks: The `-s read-only` flag was the enforcement mechanism restricting the spawned codex process to read-only operations. Without it, codex falls back to its default approval policy (suggest/auto-edit), meaning the review agent can now create, modify, or delete files in `opts.repoPath`. The caller's prompt explicitly forbids mutations ('never edit files or run mutating commands'), but that instruction is advisory to the LLM — the sandbox flag was the hard boundary. Removing it converts a sandboxed read-only reviewer into an unrestricted agent that can tamper with the very code it is reviewing.

findings.title: Removing `-s read-only` un-sandboxes the codex exec subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` (headless mode: no interactive approval, so the sandbox flag is the only write/exec boundary) with cwd=repoPath and a prompt derived from untrusted reviewed content. The base commit deliberately pinned `-s read-only`. Dropping it makes the subprocess fall back to codex's default sandbox (for `codex exec`, workspace-write rather than read-only), so a prompt-injection payload embedded in the repo under review can drive the agent to write files or run commands in the workspace/host. runCodex is an exported shared utility with no in-repo caller, so it now ships an unrestricted-exec capability to every consumer.

findings.title: Removed merge-base guard lets non-ancestor PR_BASE_SHA corrupt the diff
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code computed merge-base(baseSha, headSha) so the diff always started at the true common ancestor. The new code passes baseSha directly to git-diff. When PR_BASE_SHA is set to a commit that is NOT an ancestor of HEAD (e.g. the base-branch tip after main advanced past the PR branch point), git diff baseSha HEAD includes reverse-deltas from the base branch's post-fork commits. The review then analyses and posts inline comments on changes that are not part of the PR. The fallback path (no env var) is safe because merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) is always an ancestor, but the env-var path lost its only safety net.

findings.title: Diff uses raw PR_BASE_SHA without merge-base normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is set to the base branch tip (e.g. github.event.pull_request.base.sha) and main has advanced since the PR branched, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes reverse-diffs of commits that landed on main after the branch point. The old code computed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` first, ensuring only PR-introduced changes appeared in the patch and changedFiles. Without that normalization the review will flag files/hunks the PR never touched and post incorrect inline comments on unrelated changes.
